clue.text: Dish one has designed with ceramic base

indicators.note: a design is a fresh plan or layout, so the letters are arranged into a new pattern

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: A potter shows off a dish they have designed, complete with a ceramic base.
explanation.walkthrough: The base is the mathematical constant e, the base of natural logarithms; add it to ONE HAS CERAMIC and rearrange all fourteen letters to get MACARONI CHEESE.
explanation.definitionFit: Macaroni cheese is a baked pasta meal served as a main course, so it counts as a dish.

clue.text: Male person with weapon is soldier, perhaps

parts.note: M is the standard abbreviation for male
an archer carries a bow, a weapon

explanation.surface: An armed man is described as a soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Person with weapon' reads as a description of the soldier, but it is a separate piece: the bowman, ARCHER, after M for male.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers march on parade, so a soldier is one example of somebody who marches; 'perhaps' flags the example.

clue.text: Make usual pact — one's to split beer

parts.note: a convention is a formal agreement between states

indicators.note: splitting something opens a gap in it, so one piece goes into the middle of another

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer
one is I, and 's is short for is

explanation.surface: A drinking pact where one person has to split a beer.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s in 'one’s' stands for 'is', giving I'S, which goes inside ALE after CONVENTION.
explanation.definitionFit: To conventionalise something is to make it conform to accepted custom, turning it into the usual thing.

clue.text: One of two downfalls fitting here; don't put right answer in

definitions.text: One of two downfalls fitting here
definitions.note: a riddle pointing to the one grid-fitting downfall not ruled out

parts.words: One of two downfalls fitting here
parts.note: surface reading: two four-letter words for a downfall fit the pattern of these squares, one of them a word for a heavy shower
setter's reading: 'right' is R, 'answer' is A and 'in' is IN, which spells the rainy downfall; the instruction says not to enter that one, leaving the other

explanation.surface: A setter warns the solver that two answers fit this light and only one is correct.
explanation.walkthrough: A downfall can be a heavy fall of rain or a collapse; both RAIN and RUIN fit R?I?. R (right) + A (answer) + IN spells RAIN, which you are told not to put in, so the entry is RUIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruin names a person's or institution's collapse and disgrace, the figurative sense of a downfall.

clue.text: Stock sweet liquid extracted from pulped watermelons

indicators.note: a liquid flows and takes any shape, so the preceding letters may come in any order
pulped fruit is mashed up, so what remains is thoroughly rearranged
extracting removes material, so these letters are taken out of the longer word

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, its letters in any order

explanation.surface: Making a stock by squeezing sweet juice out of mashed watermelons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet liquid' looks like juice, but it means the letters of SWEET in any order; strike W, T, E, E, S from WATERMELONS and rearrange the leftover A, R, M, L, O, N.
explanation.definitionFit: Stock as an adjective means standard or commonplace, as in a stock response, which is what normal means.

clue.text: Redouble constant hard work and get on with it

parts.note: c is the symbol for the constant speed of light
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
op is short for opus, a work
to redouble is to do again, so the string built from the other three pieces is written a second time

explanation.surface: A boss urges staff to double their hard work and hurry up.
explanation.walkthrough: C, H and OP make CHOP, and 'Redouble' asks for it twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Chop-chop is an informal exclamation urging somebody to hurry, the same as telling them to get a move on.

clue.text: Requests a vermouth served up between courses

indicators.note: something placed between sits inside, with material on both sides

parts.note: entrées are courses of a meal
taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue something served up is raised, so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: It is short for Italian vermouth, as in gin and It

explanation.surface: A glass of vermouth is brought to the table between courses at dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: IT is crossword shorthand for Italian vermouth. A plus IT upside down gives ATI, which sits inside ENTREES.
explanation.definitionFit: Entreaties are earnest pleas or appeals, so the plural noun matches requests.

clue.text: Train second side, not all there on ground

parts.note: s is the abbreviation for second
a side in sport is a team
not all there means mad, which is loco
ground in the sense of reason is a motive; 'on' places it after

explanation.surface: A coach drills the second team, whose members seem not quite with it on the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not all there' is one idiom meaning crazy, giving LOCO; 'ground' means a reason, giving MOTIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: A steam locomotive is the engine that pulls carriages, and loosely stands for the whole railway vehicle.

clue.text: European city that is attractive

parts.note: Bonn is a German city, once the West German capital
i.e. abbreviates id est, that is

explanation.surface: A European city described as attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That is' reads as a joining phrase but supplies IE, the abbreviation of Latin id est.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonnie is a Scottish and northern English word for pretty or good-looking.

clue.text: More liquid one fed to climbing plant

indicators.note: food fed to something goes inside it, so one piece ends up within another

parts.note: a runner bean climbs up canes
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A gardener gives more liquid feed to a climbing plant.
explanation.walkthrough: The runner is the runner bean, a climbing vegetable grown up poles in British gardens.
explanation.definitionFit: Runnier is the comparative of runny, flowing more freely, so it matches more liquid.

clue.text: Busy male close to stopping, aware of limits

indicators.note: limits are boundaries that enclose, so one piece is held within another

parts.note: to be on to something is to be aware of it
he is the male pronoun

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is kept

parts.note: last letter of stopping

explanation.surface: A busy man, about to stop, knows his limits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Limits' reads as a noun about the man's capacity, but it is a verb: the phrase for being wise to a scheme encloses the rest. Note the enumeration splits the letters differently from the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: On the go is an idiom for constantly active, always doing something, which is being busy.

clue.text: Bladed items airline, possibly, reported

indicators.note: a report is something spoken, so the word is taken by how it is said rather than spelt

parts.note: a hose is a line that can carry air, as at a garage

explanation.surface: A report about what an airline allows as bladed items in luggage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Airline' is not a carrier of passengers but a tube carrying air, a hose; 'possibly' flags it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoe is a gardening tool with a flat metal blade on a long handle for weeding.

clue.text: Critical journalist blasted the match with article

indicators.note: something blasted is blown apart, so these letters are scattered and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A sports writer tears into the game in a scathing piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' here is the grammatical kind, AN, not a newspaper piece as the journalist suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: A hatchet man is a writer employed to savage people or works in print, a vicious critic.

clue.text: Carrot stick with covering of peanut oil oddly ignored

indicators.note: in a down clue a covering sits on top, so one piece goes above the other
ignoring the odd-numbered letters leaves only the even ones

parts.note: second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters
to stick things together is to cement them

explanation.surface: A carrot stick coated in peanut oil, where the oil is somehow left out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carrot stick' reads as a snack, but carrot is the definition and stick is a verb, CEMENT, topped by the even letters of 'peanut oil'.
explanation.definitionFit: A carrot is an incentive dangled to persuade someone, as in carrot and stick, which is an enticement.

clue.text: Full barrel in bar

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it

parts.note: a rod is a bar
a tun is a large cask

explanation.surface: A full barrel standing in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub, which suits the barrel, but it means a metal rod.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotund describes a plump, rounded figure, and full can mean well-filled out in shape, as in a full face.

clue.text: Opening of craft beverage with pronounced sound

parts.note: port is a fortified wine

indicators.note: to pronounce is to say out loud, so the word goes by its spoken form

parts.note: sound means intact or whole

explanation.surface: Opening a craft beer with a loud popping noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craft beverage' suggests craft beer, but craft is a boat and 'Opening of craft' is the definition; 'pronounced' looks like 'marked' but signals the sound change.
explanation.definitionFit: A porthole is the round window set in the side of a ship, an opening in a vessel's hull.

clue.text: Went on large shed from rickety bird table

indicators.note: a rickety structure is shaky and falling apart, so the letters are rebuilt in a new order
what is shed is cast off, so a letter is dropped from the longer phrase

parts.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A large shed is too close to a wobbly bird table in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shed' looks like a garden building beside the bird table, but it is a verb meaning cast off. To rabbit on is British slang for chattering at length.
explanation.definitionFit: To rabbit is informal British for talking on and on, so rabbited means went on in the chattering sense.

clue.text: Whizz kid almost entirely rejected the French waster

indicators.note: almost all of something means everything but the very end

parts.note: a prodigy is a gifted child

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so it reads in the opposite direction

parts.note: la is French for the (feminine)

explanation.surface: A young genius spurned by the French is written off as a waster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejected the French' sounds like a snub from France, but it just turns the French word for 'the' backwards; 'almost entirely' clips only the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Prodigal used as a noun means a spendthrift who squanders money, from the parable of the prodigal son.

clue.text: Uniform leaves in tree

indicators.note: to leave is to go away, so the named letter departs from the word

parts.note: to be in is to be fashionable or popular
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A uniform made of leaves in a tree, perhaps a forest costume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' suggests foliage beside the tree, but it is a verb: U departs from POPULAR, which is what 'in' means.
explanation.definitionFit: The poplar is a tall, fast-growing deciduous tree of the willow family.

clue.text: Crook admitting penitency at last over past

indicators.note: admitting someone lets them inside, so one piece is held within another

parts.note: a crook is a bend or curve, as in the crook of the arm

indicators.note: at last points to the end of a word, so only its final letter is used

parts.note: last letter of penitency
O is the cricket scorebook abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: A criminal finally shows remorse about his past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crook' tempts as a criminal, but it is a bend; O for over comes from cricket scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: Beyond and past are both prepositions meaning further than or on the far side of a point.

clue.text: Policeman tense arresting Scotsman and Geordie, perhaps …

indicators.note: to arrest is to seize and hold someone, so one piece is held within another

parts.note: DI is a Detective Inspector
T is the grammar abbreviation for tense
Alec is a Scottish form of Alexander

explanation.surface: A tense policeman arrests a Scot and a man from Newcastle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Geordie' seems to be a second suspect, but it is the definition. A Geordie is someone from Newcastle upon Tyne, and Geordie is also the name of that area's speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Geordie is the regional variety of English spoken on Tyneside, one example of a dialect.

clue.text: … caught Scotsman, not initially Geordie fence …

parts.note: c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

indicators.note: 'not' excludes something, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: Gordon is a Scottish name and clan

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter is used

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: Continuing the arrest story: a Scot is caught, while the Newcastle man is not at first, and a fence goes up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not initially Geordie' means without G, the first letter of Geordie, so G comes off GORDON.
explanation.definitionFit: A cordon is a line of police or barriers keeping people back, a kind of fence or barrier.

clue.text: Collection of petitions: Restore poor bakery

indicators.note: restoring something rebuilds it, so the letters are put back together in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Campaigners gather petitions to save a struggling bakery.
explanation.walkthrough: The petitions are prayers, not signed campaign documents, and 'poor' belongs to the letters, not the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: A prayer book gathers prayers, which are petitions addressed to God, into one volume.

clue.text: Drink that perissodactyl has

indicators.note: something one word has is contained in it, so the answer sits among its letters

parts.note: letters six to nine

explanation.surface: A drink favoured by a horse or rhino.
explanation.walkthrough: A perissodactyl is an odd-toed hoofed mammal such as a horse; the long word is just a carrier.
explanation.definitionFit: Soda is fizzy water or a sweet carbonated soft drink.

clue.text: … Cockney trio released

indicators.note: a Cockney accent turns the 'th' sound into 'f', so the word is taken as a Londoner says it

parts.note: a trio is three, which a Cockney voices with an f sound at the start

explanation.surface: The ellipsis closes the story: the fenced-in Cockney trio are let go.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys are working-class East Londoners whose accent says 'free' for 'three'.
explanation.definitionFit: Released and free both describe someone let out of custody or captivity.

clue.text: Least productive outings at stores

indicators.note: to store something is to keep it inside, so one piece holds another

parts.note: taken as written
rides are trips out

explanation.surface: Shopping trips turn out to be the least productive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stores' looks like shops for the outings, but it is a verb: AT stores RIDES.
explanation.definitionFit: Arid land yields no crops, so the aridest is the most barren, and figuratively the least fruitful.

clue.text: Rodents take from kitchen regularly

parts.note: to do drugs is to take them

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: Mice and their kin raiding the kitchen for food on a regular basis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' looks like a link word pointing at the kitchen, but it belongs to the letter string: the even letters run across both words.
explanation.definitionFit: Dormice are small, bushy-tailed, hibernating rodents found in European woodland.

clue.text: Insecure teen's tried on garment for personal benefit

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another comes after it

parts.note: a vest is an undergarment, or a waistcoat in American English

indicators.note: something insecure is unstable and not fixed, so the letters shift into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An anxious teenager tries on clothes for their own sake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tried on garment' reads as trying on clothes, but 'on' only places the anagram after VEST.
explanation.definitionFit: A vested interest is a personal stake in an outcome, a reason to benefit oneself from it.
